title: Meccan Architecture Overview
description: Mecca sits in a hot, arid valley in western Saudi Arabia, and its architecture answers that valley first: thick walls against heat, shaded courtyards and streets against sun, and ventilation that moves air without machines. The older city grew as dense, low- to mid-rise quarters of stone and coral houses around narrow, shaded lanes, with the Grand Mosque at its centre. The modern city keeps that centre and adds high-rise hotels and towers around it, so the skyline now reads as two layers at once: a historic fabric of courtyard houses and a modern ring of tall buildings serving pilgrims. Materials tell the same story in sequence. Coral stone and timber came from the Red Sea coast and from trade, mud and stone came from the valley itself, and concrete, steel, and glass arrived with modern construction. Each material shaped what builders could do: coral and stone carry thick load-bearing walls, timber makes the projecting lattice screens called rawashin, and concrete and steel make the tall, wide-span structures of the modern ring possible. No single material defines Meccan architecture; the sequence of materials does. This pair describes buildings in general, factual terms, with published figures where they exist and ranges where sources differ. It contains no depiction of any person, and its diagrams are original geometric drawings of arches, domes, and plans only. Where the record touches devotional life, it labels that material tradition and keeps it apart from measured building facts.

title: Traditional Hijazi Houses: Rawashin and Coral Stone
description: Hijazi houses are the traditional town houses of the Red Sea coast, built in Mecca, Jeddah, and neighbouring towns from coral stone walls and timber details. Their most recognisable feature is the rawshan, a projecting wooden lattice bay window that shades the room behind it, catches breezes, and lets occupants look out onto the street while remaining screened from it. Rawashin are built from turned and carved timber, often painted, and they project over the street, so a row of them turns a narrow lane into a shaded, decorated corridor. Coral stone, cut from fossil coral along the coast, makes thick walls that hold their cool through the hot day and release it slowly at night, and the stone is finished with lime plaster that protects it from rain and salt air. Timber also appears in doors, ceilings, and staircases, often carved and studded, while interior rooms open onto a central space that draws air through the house. The house is therefore a climate machine before it is a decoration: mass for coolness, projection for shade, lattice for air, and a plan that pulls breezes through. Many historic Hijazi houses have been lost to redevelopment, and those that survive are now the focus of conservation work, described in the conservation record of this pair. Descriptions here are general and factual, drawn from published architectural histories, and no individual house is claimed to survive unless a conservation source says so.

title: Courtyard Houses of Mecca
description: The courtyard house turns a house inward. Rooms face a central open court rather than the street, so family life has daylight and air without opening the house to the lane, and the court itself becomes a shaded, planted room for much of the day. In Mecca's climate the court works by shade and stack effect: sun heats the air in the court, warm air rises, and cooler air is drawn in through shaded openings, so the house breathes even when the street outside is still and hot. Courts vary in size with the wealth and plot of the household, from small light-wells that serve mainly for air and light to generous planted courts with a well or cistern, seating, and trees. Rooms around the court are arranged by use and by season: summer rooms on the shaded side, winter rooms catching the low sun, and roof terraces used for sleeping and gathering on hot nights. The plan is flexible because the court, not the facade, is the house's centre. Modern apartments in Mecca rarely reproduce the full courtyard, but the idea survives in atria, light-wells, and shaded internal courts in larger buildings, where the same logic, daylight and air from within, serves a different building type. The courtyard is therefore both a historic house form and a continuing design idea, and this pair treats it as both.

title: Tower Houses of Mecca
description: Tower houses rise several storeys above their neighbours, often on a small plot, and they answer a crowded historic city where land near the centre is scarce. Building up gives a household more rooms without a larger plot, and the upper floors catch breezes that never reach the shaded lanes below, so height is a climate answer as well as a density answer. Lower floors are often the most solid, with thick walls and small openings, while upper floors open wider with rawashin and balconies. Structurally, a tower house is a stack of load-bearing walls, with timber floors and a timber roof, and its stability comes from wall thickness and from the way floors tie the walls together. Stairs climb within the tower, sometimes in a corner stairwell, and each floor may hold one or two rooms, so the house reads as a vertical sequence of rooms rather than a horizontal spread. Water, storage, and service rooms sit low, living rooms sit high, and the roof serves as an outdoor room. Tower houses also shape the street: a row of them makes a lane feel like a canyon, shaded for most of the day, with the sky appearing as a narrow strip above. That shade is a public benefit of private height, and it is one reason historic Meccan lanes, for all their narrowness, were walkable even in summer heat.

title: The Ottoman Architectural Layer in Mecca
description: From the sixteenth century, when the Hijaz came under Ottoman rule, Mecca gained an Ottoman layer of building: domes, arches, and stonework in the imperial manner, added to mosques, schools, fountains, and public works. Ottoman builders worked in stone and brick, used lead-covered domes and pencil minarets in some settings, and brought a repertoire of arches, muqarnas (stalactite-like corbelling), and tiled or painted decoration that sits visibly alongside the local coral-stone tradition. The layer is not a replacement of Hijazi building but an addition to it, and older and Ottoman elements stand in the same quarters. The Grand Mosque precinct carries the clearest Ottoman traces in its arcades, domes, and minarets from successive Ottoman works, although later Saudi expansions have rebuilt and enlarged much of the precinct around them. Outside the precinct, Ottoman schools, fortifications on the surrounding hills, and public fountains mark the period in the wider city. Dating any single element precisely needs a building-by-building survey, and this record therefore describes the Ottoman layer in general terms rather than assigning dates to individual features without a source. The value of naming the layer is that it stops a reader from reading Mecca as a single period. The city is a stack of periods, Hijazi, Ottoman, and modern, and each period's buildings answer the same valley and the same pilgrimage with the materials and styles of their own time.

title: Modern High-Rise Building Around the Haram
description: The modern ring around the Grand Mosque precinct answers a numbers problem: millions of pilgrims need lodging, services, and circulation within walking distance of the mosque, and the valley floor is narrow. Building tall puts many rooms on a small footprint, keeps walking distances short, and frees ground for plazas, gates, and transport. Hotels, residential towers, and shopping podiums now form a dense ring around the precinct, linked by bridges, tunnels, and shaded walkways that keep pilgrims moving in heat and in crowds. High-rise construction here uses reinforced concrete and steel frames, with cladding in stone, glass, and composite panels, and with deep podiums that hold shops, food halls, and prayer spaces. Crowd movement shapes the plan as much as structure does: separate flows for arrivals and departures, wide stairs and escalators, and open plazas that absorb surges after prayers. Fire safety, ventilation, and cooling at this scale are engineering systems in their own right, and the buildings are judged as much by how safely they empty as by how many rooms they hold. Critics and supporters describe this ring differently, and this record reports the factual trade-off without taking a side: height near the mosque shortens walks and increases capacity, while it also changes the historic skyline and the scale of the streets around it. Conservation and contemporary-design records in this pair carry that discussion further, in factual terms.

title: Abraj Al Bait: Height, Function, and Published Figures
description: Abraj Al Bait, also called the Makkah Royal Clock Tower complex, stands immediately beside the Grand Mosque precinct in Mecca and is a mixed-use complex of seven towers over podiums, holding hotels, residences, shopping, and prayer and service spaces. Its centrepiece, the Makkah Royal Clock Tower, is reported at 601 metres architectural height with 120 floors, completed and opened in 2012, and some listings give a tip height of 607 metres including the spire, which is why sources differ: architectural height and tip height are different measurements of the same tower. This record states both and labels the difference, as of 2026-10-26. The complex's published total floor area is about 1.5 to 1.6 million square metres, making it one of the largest building complexes by floor area in the world, and its clock faces, about 43 metres in diameter, are reported as the largest clock faces in the world, visible from many kilometres away. The tower was developed as part of an endowment project intended to fund the operation and development of the Grand Mosque, and its hotels serve pilgrims visiting the mosque. Those purposes, hotel and endowment, explain both its scale and its position. Figures for floor counts in secondary sources sometimes disagree, with some listings counting podium or service levels differently, so this record anchors on the widely repeated figures, 601 metres architectural, 120 floors for the clock tower, 2012 opening, and states that other counts exist. A reader needing a certified figure should check the current CTBUH or developer listing, because tall-building figures are revised when measurement standards change.

title: Materials: Stone, Coral, Wood, and Concrete
description: Stone is Mecca's oldest building material in the valley itself: local stone, cut and laid in thick walls, carries load, stores coolness, and weathers slowly. Coral stone, brought from the Red Sea coast, is lighter and more porous, and it was the wall material of the Hijazi town house, finished in lime plaster that sealed its pores against rain and salt. Both stones work by mass: a thick stone wall delays heat, so the inside of a house stays cooler through the afternoon than a thin wall would. Wood is the detail material: teak and other imported hardwoods, brought by Red Sea trade, made rawashin, doors, ceilings, and mashrabiya screens, and their carving and turning carry much of the visual richness of Hijazi houses. Wood moves with humidity and needs paint and repair, so timber elements are the parts of a historic house that are most often replaced, and conservation of a Hijazi house is often conservation of its timber as much as of its stone. Concrete, steel, and glass are the modern materials: concrete frames carry tall buildings, steel spans wide halls and bridges, and glass brings daylight into deep plans, at the cost of heat gain that must then be cooled mechanically. A materials record is also a trade record. Stone is local, coral is coastal, timber is imported, and concrete and steel are industrial, and each shift in material marks a shift in what Mecca could build and what it could afford. The modern ring could not exist in coral and timber, and the historic quarters could not have been built in concrete without losing the very qualities, mass and shade, that made them work.

title: Climate-Responsive Design: Shade, Ventilation, and Thick Walls
description: Mecca's climate is hot and arid, with long, intensely sunny summers, and its traditional architecture is a set of passive answers to that climate. Shade comes first: narrow lanes, projecting upper floors, rawashin, awnings, and courtyard walls all keep sun off walls, windows, and walking routes, so shade is treated as a building element, not as an afterthought. A shaded wall can be many degrees cooler than a sunlit wall of the same material, and a shaded street is walkable where a sunlit street is not. Ventilation comes second, and it works with shade rather than against it. Openings are placed to catch prevailing breezes and to let warm air escape high, through courts, stairwells, and roof openings, while lattice screens break direct sun but let air pass. Thick walls come third: stone and coral mass absorb daytime heat and release it at night, flattening the indoor temperature swing so rooms stay liveable through the afternoon peak. Together, shade, air, and mass let a house stay comfortable with little or no mechanical cooling. Modern buildings in Mecca use the same three ideas in new forms: deep shading fins and screens on glass facades, shaded podiums and walkways, and insulated mass walls, alongside mechanical cooling for spaces that passive means alone cannot serve. The continuity matters for conservation: a historic house stripped of its shade devices and fitted with air conditioning alone loses both its appearance and its original climate logic.

title: Arches and Domes in Meccan Building
description: The arch is the working shape of Meccan masonry: a curved span that turns vertical load into compression along the curve, so stone and brick, which are strong in compression and weak in tension, can span an opening without a timber lintel. Meccan buildings use several arch profiles, from the semicircular arch to the pointed arch, which rises higher for the same span and pushes less sideways on its supports, and to the horseshoe and ogee profiles that appear as decoration as well as structure. Arcades of repeated arches carry the upper walls of mosque precincts and market streets, turning a long wall into a rhythm of openings. The dome extends the arch in all directions, covering a square or circular space with a curved shell that, in its simplest form, is a hemisphere. Domes in Mecca appear over mosque spaces, tombs, and pavilions, often raised on a drum with windows that light the space below, and often finished in lead, plaster, or tile. A dome's geometry decides its behaviour: a shallow dome pushes outward hard on its supports, a tall dome pushes more downward, and builders answer outward push with thick walls, buttresses, or iron ties hidden in the masonry. Diagrams in this pair are original geometric drawings of arches and domes only, with no human figures and no copied images. They show span, rise, radius, and arc length, the four numbers that let a reader check an arch or a dome on paper, and the demo below computes them for a model arch. Real historic arches vary with stone size, mortar, and settlement, so model numbers are a teaching aid, not a survey of any individual building.

title: Minaret Styles in Mecca
description: A minaret is a tall, slender tower from which the call to prayer is announced, and Mecca's minarets show more than one style because they were built in more than one period. Ottoman-period minarets tend toward the slender pencil form: a square or polygonal base, a tapering cylindrical shaft, one or more balconies, and a pointed conical cap. Later Saudi-period minarets around the Grand Mosque precinct are taller and broader, built in concrete with stone cladding, and designed to read clearly across a vast precinct and a dense ring of high-rise buildings. Minaret design balances height, proportion, and structure. Height carries the call and marks the mosque on the skyline, but a taller tower catches more wind and needs a broader base and a stiffer shaft, and balconies must be reached by internal stairs that fit within the shaft. Proportion is the visible result: a minaret that is too thin for its height looks fragile, one that is too thick looks heavy, and builders in each period found their own working ratio between base width and total height. Minarets are described here in general, architectural terms, with no claim about any individual tower's height unless a published source gives it. A reader who wants exact heights should check the current precinct or tall-building listings, because minaret counts and heights change with each precinct expansion.

title: Gates and Walls of Old Mecca
description: Old Mecca, like many walled towns, was entered through gates in a defensive wall that followed the valley's edges and the quarters it protected. Gates controlled who and what entered, marked the boundary between the town and the road beyond it, and gave their names to the quarters and routes around them, so a gate name often survives in a street or district name long after the gate itself is gone. Walls and gates also shaped trade: goods entering the town passed through gates where they could be counted, taxed, and directed to markets. Little of the old wall circuit survives as a continuous structure, because the modern city has grown far beyond it and rebuilt over its line, but gates survive as places and as names, and the Grand Mosque precinct has its own named gates that organise pilgrim movement today. Those modern precinct gates are functional architecture: wide, clearly signed, and designed for crowd flow, with separate handling for arrivals, departures, and emergencies. The old defensive idea, control at a threshold, thus continues in a new form, crowd management at a gate. This record describes gates and walls in general terms and does not assign surviving fabric to a specific gate without a conservation source. Where the public record is silent about a particular gate's survival, this record says so rather than guessing.

title: Conservation and Heritage in Mecca
description: Conservation in Mecca faces a sharp tension: the historic quarters hold coral-stone houses, lanes, and craft traditions worth keeping, while pilgrimage growth demands new capacity, wider circulation, and modern services on the same ground. Conservation practice therefore works on several levels at once: recording buildings before they are altered, protecting the most significant survivors, reusing historic houses for cultural or hospitality uses where that keeps them maintained, and rebuilding lost details from measured drawings and photographs when rebuilding is chosen. The technical problems are specific to the materials. Coral stone decays when its lime plaster fails and salt air reaches it, timber rawashin rot and are eaten by insects if paint and drainage fail, and roofs leak when their traditional waterproofing is replaced carelessly. Conservation that replaces coral with concrete block, or a carved rawshan with a flat aluminium screen, keeps the outline but loses the material, the climate behaviour, and the craft, and good conservation records say so plainly rather than calling a replica an original. Heritage in Mecca is also a living question, not only a buildings question: the craftspeople who can carve a rawshan, lay coral stone, and mix lime plaster are part of the heritage, and training new craftspeople is conservation work as much as repairing a wall is. This record states no conservation status for any individual building unless a published conservation source gives it, and it treats every claim about survival as checkable or as explicitly unconfirmed.

title: Contemporary Saudi Architecture in Mecca
description: Contemporary Saudi architecture in Mecca works with the modern ring's scale but increasingly reuses traditional devices: deep screens that recall the rawshan, shaded courtyards and atria, stone cladding that recalls coral and local stone, and geometric patterning drawn from historic decoration. The aim, as stated by designers in published project descriptions, is to make tall, air-conditioned buildings that still read as belonging to Mecca rather than to any city anywhere, and to give pilgrims shaded, legible routes between lodging and mosque. Newer projects also answer sustainability pressures that the historic city never faced at this scale: cooling loads for millions of visitors, water use, and the waste and transport of a pilgrimage city. Design responses include shaded facades that cut solar gain, district cooling, water recycling, and transport planning that keeps private cars out of the precinct core. Whether any individual project meets its stated goals is a question for its own post-occupancy reporting, and this record does not certify projects it has not measured. The contemporary layer is still being written, and this record treats it as open rather than settled: new towers, stations, and public spaces continue to change the precinct, and a record dated 2026-10-26 will need updating as they open. That openness is stated here rather than hidden, so a later reader can see what was known when this record was written.

title: Architecture Glossary
description: Arcade: a row of arches carried on columns or piers, forming a covered walkway. Arch: a curved masonry span that carries load in compression. Buttress: a masonry mass that resists the outward push of an arch or dome. Coral stone: fossil coral cut as a building stone, used for Hijazi town-house walls and finished in lime plaster. Courtyard: an open court within a building, giving light, air, and shade to the rooms around it. Dome: a curved shell roof, often a hemisphere, covering a round or square space. Drum: the cylindrical wall that raises a dome above its supporting walls and often holds windows. Muqarnas: stalactite-like corbelling that eases the transition from a square room to a round dome. Podium: the low, wide base of a tall building, holding shops and services. Rawshan (plural rawashin): a projecting wooden lattice bay window of Hijazi houses, giving shade, air, and screened outlook. The entries here are working definitions for this pair, and the full treatment of each term lives in its own record. Where a term also appears in devotional contexts, this glossary gives only its architectural meaning and points the reader to the spiritual-life pair for the devotional meaning, keeping fact and tradition in their own records.
